title: METHANE EMISSIONS FROM LANDFILLS: INTEGRATED STRATEGIES TOWARD ZERO-EMISSION WASTE AND WASTEWATER MANAGEMENT

METHANE EMISSIONS FROM LANDFILLS: INTEGRATED STRATEGIES TOWARD ZERO-EMISSION WASTE AND WASTEWATER MANAGEMENT

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Mohammed F.M. Abushammala, Siham Farrag, Sultan Almuaythir, Zaid Alajlan, Tharaa M. Al-Zghoul, and D. M. Alqahtani

ABSTRACT

Landfills are a major source of anthropogenic methane (CH4) emissions generated through the anaerobic decomposition of municipal solid waste. During the methanogenic phase, landfill gas typically contains 5560% CH₄ and 40–45% CO2. Methane generation is highly variable, with reported potential (L0) ranging from 64 to 83.4 m³ CH4/Mg and degradation rates (k) between 0.016 and 0.355 yr⁻¹. Field measurements further show strong spatial variability in methane fluxes from 0.003 to >1000 g CH4.m-2. d-1. Despite engineered controls, up to 31% of generated methane may still be emitted as fugitive losses. Methane mitigation technologies exhibit wide performance variability. Gas collection systems achieve 35–90% efficiency, while biological oxidation systems such as biocovers reach 40–90% and exceed 96% under optimized conditions, with biofilters achieving up to 100% removal. Flaring provides >99% destruction efficiency but without energy recovery. In contrast, anaerobic digestion, waste-to-energy (WtE), and LFG-to-energy systems enable simultaneous mitigation and energy recovery, achieving GHG reductions exceeding 83% and power generation between 1.6 and 47.5 MWe. Integrated systems combining gas capture, biological oxidation, and energy recovery demonstrate the highest overall performance, achieving up to 99.87% greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction and large-scale energy production exceeding 6760–8050 GWh/year. However, system performance remains highly dependent on scale, methane availability, and operational stability. Economic assessment shows that LFG-to-Energy systems achieve internal rates of return of 14.9–31.1% and payback periods of 1.314.3 years. Overall, the study demonstrates that near-zero emission landfills are achievable only through integrated systems supported by effective monitoring and enabling policy frameworks.
